newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Utd Utils seen as buy despite mgmt row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Utd Utils seen as buy despite mgmt row.

text.p: Britain's United Utilities Plc faces growing discontent over its chairman, Sir Desmond Pitcher, but investors should look past the dispute and focus on the firm's growth prospects, analysts said on Friday.
Pitcher's surprise sacking of chief executive Brian Staples last month fueled concerns about a board split and prompted some investors to demand that the 62-year-old step down as executive chairman.
Pitcher, whose hefty bonuses have ranked him among Britain's so-called corporate "fat cats", has a reputation for a hands-on management style described by some as "overbearing" and "autocratic".
"The concern is who calls the tune at United Utilities and secondly, are they singing from the same hymn sheet," said one utilities analyst.
"The name is United Utilities, but it's being perceived in a number of places as Divided Utilities," the analyst added.
The Financial Times reported on Friday that big institutional investors were calling for Pitcher to move to a non-executive post by the end of this year.
The paper's influential Lex column also lambasted Pitcher, entitling its article "Pitch him out."
Pitcher has previously said he would not resign. A company spokeswoman declined to comment.
United's shares fell 13 pence to 697.5 by 1045 GMT, but some analysts recommended buying the stock on weakness, saying the utility's outlook was strong.
Nigel Hawkins, utilities analyst at Yamaichi, rated the stock as a short-term buy with a six-month price target of about 760 pence.
"The market should focus on the underlying profit drivers, which are their water and sewerage revenues and their distribution of electricity revenues," he said.
"At the end of the day, it's a utility business with utility revenues, and it depends perhaps slightly less on management compared to some other sectors," he added.
Another analyst also recommended buying stock in United, which was formed in 1995 when North West Water took over electricity company Norweb.
"There's a lot of costs to come out of the synergies between the two businesses," the analyst said.
He added that United appeared to have limited its overseas risks after taking an 83 million pound ($132 million) charge last financial year for losses on a sewerage contract in Bangkok.
That charge, along with personal differences, may have contributed to Pitcher's push to remove Staples as chief executive and replace him with Derek Green, managing director of the utility division.
At the time, United said Staples left after "a loss of confidence in him by the board", without giving further details.

"I suspect the gap between Staples and Sir Desmond widened over a period of time," one analyst said, noting that Staples' predecessor, Bob Thian, had left the company in similar circumstances a few years ago. ($ = 0.628 British Pounds)
